In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the spatial frequency content in the scene is a crucial parameter in scene categorization for AMD patients and that the HSF content is the one that needs the higher luminance contrast to be processed.
AMD patients can categorize scenes in LSF and HFS conditions, but they do it less accurately than healthy participants, and the accuracy of their categorization is improved when the HSF are enhanced.
AMD patients have a preserved LSF processing in their parafovea and this allows them to categorize scenes efficiently.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in order to improve visual scene perception in AMD patients, we have to take into account the spatial frequency content and the luminance contrast of scenes.

the HSF deficit in AMD patients could be partially overcome by increasing the contrast level of HSF scenes, which is consistent with the fact that HSF are generally less visible than LSF in natural scenes.
the spatial frequency processing deficit in AMD patients could be partially restored when the visual system is exposed to high luminance contrasts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
scene perception is possible in the residual vision of AMD patients.
the visual system of AMD patients is still able to process spatial frequency content in residual vision, but the ability to do it efficiently is limited.

, even with a severe central vision loss, patients with AMD are able to categorize large natural scenes in their peripheral vision, provided that they have access to the spatial frequency content and luminance contrast of scenes.
